summary: HFCL makes the glass fibre cables that carry internet data, plus telecom equipment and defence electronics.
description: Phone calls, video, cloud services and AI programs all reach you as pulses of light along hair-thin strands of glass called optical fibre. HFCL makes that fibre, wraps many strands into protected cables, and makes the equipment at the ends of the network, such as Wi-Fi systems, routers and radio links. Its customers are phone companies, very large technology companies that run data centres, governments and armed forces. It also makes defence electronics such as thermal sights and radars, and builds telecom networks to order. Its factories are in Hyderabad, Goa, Chennai and Hosur.
money: HFCL earns money when customers pay for the cables and equipment it ships, and for network-building work under contract. Its costs are the glass and plastic materials for fibre and cable, factory running costs, engineers and research, and interest on loans. Large orders take months to make and deliver, so HFCL spends before it is paid.
customers: Telecom companies buy cables and equipment to build and expand their networks. Hyperscalers are the very large technology companies that run huge data centres; they buy fibre cables and connection products in large quantities. Government agencies and armed forces buy network and defence equipment. HFCL says most of its customers are private companies and that a large and growing share of its sales goes to customers abroad.
drivers: How much fibre and equipment customers order, the prices they pay, how well the factories are used, what raw materials cost, and whether big orders are delivered and paid for on time.

groups.title: Optical fibre and cables
groups.examples: Optical fibre, cables for telecom networks, fibre-to-the-home cables and cables for data centres.
groups.explanation: Optical fibre is a thin strand of glass that carries data as pulses of light. A cable bundles many fibres in protective layers so it can be laid underground or hung from poles. A cable maker earns money by making many kilometres of fibre and cable at a cost lower than the selling price.

groups.title: Connectivity products for data centres
groups.examples: Cable assemblies, connectors, patch panels and splitters.
groups.explanation: A data centre is a building full of computers. Thousands of fibre links inside it must be connected, organised and protected. Hyperscalers building new data centres need large numbers of these parts, which is why HFCL has approved building a dedicated factory for them.

groups.title: Telecom equipment
groups.examples: Wi-Fi access points, routers and wireless links for mobile networks.
groups.explanation: A router is a device that sends data to the right place. A backhaul radio is a wireless link that carries traffic from a mobile tower to the rest of the network. HFCL says this equipment is built on its own design and technology that it owns.

groups.title: Defence and aerospace equipment
groups.examples: Thermal weapon sights, electronic fuzes, surveillance radars, radio links, wire harnesses and planned ammunition manufacturing.
groups.explanation: Thermal sights show heat instead of light. An electronic fuze is the part of a shell or grenade that controls when it works. Armed forces buy such equipment through government procurement, with long approval times and large but irregular orders. HFCL says it is setting up an ammunition manufacturing complex and has proposed to buy an aerospace business; the lesson treats both as plans until they are completed.

groups.title: Building networks to order
groups.examples: Fibre networks, mobile backhaul, rural networks and government programmes such as BharatNet.
groups.explanation: System integration means designing, building and testing a network for a customer. BharatNet is a government programme to connect villages with fibre. HFCL says it is moving away from high-volume building work towards products that earn better returns and need less cash.

basics.title: What is an order book?
basics.text: An order book is the total value of confirmed orders that have not yet been delivered. It shows demand that is already booked. It is not revenue yet, because the goods still have to be made, delivered and accepted, and orders can be delayed or changed.

basics.title: Why is a customer’s size a risk as well as an opportunity?
basics.text: A single very large customer can fill the factories and lift sales. If that customer slows its orders, changes supplier or delays payment, the effect on a company of HFCL’s size can be large.

basics.title: What does making your own glass rod mean?
basics.text: Optical fibre is drawn from a glass rod called a preform. HFCL is building a factory to make preform itself, instead of buying it. This is called backward integration: moving back along the supply chain to make a part you currently buy. It can lower costs and reduce shortages, but it needs money and skill up front.

steps.title: Win an order
steps.text: A telecom company, cloud company, government body or armed force places an order or signs a supply agreement, sometimes for several years.

steps.title: Make the fibre
steps.text: Glass preform is heated and drawn into fibre. Strands are coated, tested and wound onto reels.

steps.title: Build cables and equipment
steps.text: Fibre is covered with protective layers to make cables. Separate factories make routers, radios, Wi-Fi systems and defence electronics.

steps.title: Deliver, install and get accepted
steps.text: Customers check that what arrives meets their specification. For network projects, work is installed and tested before it is accepted.

steps.title: Invoice and collect
steps.text: HFCL bills the customer. Some customers pay on delivery; large projects and government orders may pay in stages or later.

specifics.title: One very large customer can change the picture
specifics.text: HFCL’s FY 2025–26 report describes a five-year cable supply agreement with a leading global hyperscaler. Exports rose from a small share of sales to more than half in the quarter to June 2026. This helps growth, but it also means HFCL depends on fewer, larger customers.

specifics.title: Growth rates can look huge after a weak year
specifics.text: In April–June 2025 HFCL was making a loss. When the next year’s quarter is compared with that low starting point, the percentage rises look very large. Look at the actual level of profit and margins in later quarters, not just the growth rate.

specifics.title: An order book is a promise, not revenue
specifics.text: HFCL reported its largest order book ever, several times its previous year’s revenue. Orders are delivered over years and may be delayed, so the order book shows potential, not the next year’s sales.

specifics.title: Defence expansion is partly still a plan
specifics.text: The ammunition complex is being set up and the aerospace purchase is proposed. Until a factory is running and an acquisition is completed, they do not yet produce earnings.

watch: How dependent is HFCL on a few very large customers?
Sales that rely on a few customers can swing sharply if one changes its plans.

Look in the annual report and results notes for the share of sales from the largest customers, the split between exports and India, and how long the main supply agreements run. Check what happens if a customer reduces orders.
Are orders turning into delivered goods and cash?
An order book only helps if it is delivered and paid for.

Compare the order book with each quarter’s revenue, and look at receivables, which are bills issued but not yet paid, and cash from operations. Note delivery delays, cancelled orders and projects that pay late.
Are the new factories ready and will they be used?
Extra capacity costs money before it earns any.
Read the progress of fibre, cable and preform expansion and the data-centre products plant. Compare capacity added with orders, and check spending on equipment against cash generated.
Is defence turning into reliable earnings?
Defence orders can be large but irregular and slow to be approved and paid.
Look for defence revenue shown separately, the status of the proposed aerospace purchase, and how long customers take to pay. Check which parts are planned and which already produce sales.
Do profit margins hold when growth settles?
A very strong quarter after a weak one may not repeat.

Compare operating profit margin across several quarters, prices of cables and the cost of glass and other materials. Check how much profit comes from one-off orders and how much from regular business.
risks: A big customer cuts back or changes supplier
A small number of large buyers account for much of growth, so losing or reducing one has a big effect.
If many makers add capacity, prices can drop, which reduces what is left after costs.
Expansion plans run late or over budget
New factories and the proposed acquisition need approvals, equipment and skilled people, and may take longer or cost more than planned.
Government and defence orders are delayed
Public-sector customers can take a long time to approve orders and pay.
A large share of sales is abroad, so exchange-rate changes and trade rules matter more than before.
context: July 2026: sales more than doubled after a weak year, and exports passed half of sales

HFCL’s 22 July 2026 results release says revenue for April–June 2026 was more than twice that of a year earlier, and exports made up more than half of revenue, compared with about a quarter a year before. A year earlier the company had made a loss and this quarter it made a profit, so the growth percentages look very large. It reported its largest order book yet, and said the proposed aerospace purchase and an ammunition complex were still being developed. These are unaudited quarterly results, not yet fully checked by auditors. The full-year figures at the end of this page cover an earlier period.
quiz: If a company’s order book is several times last year’s revenue, will next year’s revenue be that many times higher?

No. Orders are delivered over several years, may be delayed or changed, and revenue is counted only when goods are delivered and accepted. The order book shows booked demand, not guaranteed next-year sales.

financialNotes.title: Read a fast-growing manufacturer’s numbers in context
financialNotes.text: Compare revenue with operating profit, then look at cash from operations, bills not yet paid and spending on new factories. Check which year each growth rate is compared with, and how much comes from exports and one-off orders.
